Issued at 117 AM EST Sun Nov 8 2026

             -----------Synoptic Overview-----------

An impressive mid-level shortwave over New England drove a weak 
cold front through Florida on Saturday. This evening's Cape 
Canaveral sounding revealed substantial mid-level drying behind 
the front, with 700-mb relative humidity falling to just 4%. A 
broad area of high pressure extends from West Virginia to 
Oklahoma. Winds have turned northwesterly behind the front but 
will quickly turn onshore as the high remains north of Central 
Florida over the next couple of days.

The upper-level pattern across CONUS is quasi-zonal with split-flow
characteristics. A weak subtropical jet extends from Mexico to
N Florida, and the polar jet runs from the Pacific Northwest
to the Great Lakes with multiple shortwaves embedded within
it. Through early Wednesday, we anticipate little change to this
rather progressive, low-amplitude pattern. Total moisture values
should average near to just below normal with boundary-layer temps
slightly above normal. Overall, this portends high confidence in
low impacts for Florida and surrounding areas.

While the overall longwave pattern remains relatively stationary
over the next 7-9 days, substantial amplification is favored in
the latest ensemble guidance. A series of shortwaves embedded
within a 150-200 kt Pacific jet is forecast to deepen the trough
over the Eastern Pacific by Wednesday; in response, pronounced
downstream ridging should build across the Intermountain West. This
configuration, coupled with a developing -NAO blocking pattern
over Greenland, will favor the amplification of a deep trough
across the Eastern U.S. beginning Thursday.

Cluster analysis of the 07/12Z ensemble suite revealed increasing
disagreement with timing and depth of the trough by Friday and
Saturday. Before then, there is generally good agreement that a 
cold front will pass through the state sometime between late 
Thursday and early Friday. A weak subtropical jet streak may 
provide additional upper-level support for precipitation along the
boundary. However, recent runs have trended somewhat drier. Well 
north of Florida, a nor'easter may form on the eastern flank of 
the trough, enhancing northerly winds and cold air advection 
behind the front.

Guidance slightly favors a more progressive scenario with height
rises commencing next Sunday. By that time, continental high
pressure should be centered roughly over the Ohio Valley, with
winds turning onshore shortly afterward.

             -------Sensible Weather & Impacts-------

Today - Wednesday...

This is the tranquil, pleasant stretch of the forecast. Rain
chances remain below 20% for much of the period. Near-seasonable
temperatures are forecast with intervals of cloud cover mixed with
sunshine. Each day, highs will range from 80-85 with lows mainly
in the 60s, except some upper 50s north of Orlando.

A lingering easterly long-period swell persists in the Atlantic,
so the high risk of life-threatening rip currents will continue
through at least Monday. Additionally, minor coastal flooding
is possible mainly near and south of St. Lucie Inlet during the
morning high tide cycles through early this week.

Thursday - Next Weekend...

Clouds should increase Thursday as a stream of moisture precedes
an approaching cold front. Thursday's highs in the upper 70s to
near 80 will be the warmest of this period. By Thursday night,
the cold front is expected to enter Central Florida before quickly
passing south of here on Friday. Rainfall potential has trended
downward. Nearly 75% of grand ensemble members produce little to
no rainfall, or only light, scattered showers along the front.

Any lingering showers on Friday should exit the area as much drier
and cooler air drifts over the state as the weekend arrives. Highs
are forecast to range from the upper 60s to mid 70s as we end the
work week. The coolest day appears to be Saturday, when much of 
the area is forecast to only reach the mid/upper 60s. Sunday looks
a touch warmer, in the upper 60s to mid 70s.

While substantial uncertainty remains regarding the amplitude and
progression of the upper-level trough, confidence is increasing
that the coolest temperatures of the autumn season will arrive next
weekend. On the coolest morning (next Sunday), we are forecasting
mid to upper 40s over much of the interior, with low/mid 50s
along the coast. Our cooler scenario (10% chance of occurrence)
has trended slightly colder for next Sunday, ranging from the low
to mid 40s over the interior to the upper 40s and low 50s along
the coast. Accounting for wind chill, there is a 10-30% chance
of apparent temperatures in the upper 30s both next Saturday and
Sunday mornings roughly from Orlando and points northward.
